pageCopy.aboutTitle: What this assessment is — and is not
isItems: A structured way to reflect on five important areas of relationship health.
A starting point for honest conversation and intentional change.
Free to complete, with no sign-up required.
isntItems: A clinical diagnosis or validated psychometric assessment.
A definitive judgement on you, your partner, or your relationship.
Advice on whether you should stay in or leave a relationship.
A substitute for professional support or an appropriate safety assessment.

safeExitParagraphs: You do not need to complete this assessment or decide the future of your relationship right now. Consider seeking confidential individual support from a suitably qualified professional who understands relationship abuse.
If you are in immediate danger, contact local emergency services or move to a safer place if you can do so safely.
Couples therapy may not be appropriate where coercion, intimidation or abuse is present.

selfAudit.name: The Relationship Self-Audit
selfAudit.headline: Answer honestly, based on how you usually think, feel and behave in relationships.
selfAudit.metaDescription: A free self-audit across five areas that can influence relationship health: self-knowledge, emotional regulation, inherited patterns, capacity and readiness, and conflict and repair.
selfAudit.siblingBlurb: Reflect on five areas that can influence relationship health: self-knowledge, emotional regulation, inherited patterns, capacity and readiness, and conflict and repair.
intro: This self-audit helps you reflect on five areas that can influence relationship health: self-knowledge, emotional regulation, inherited patterns, capacity and readiness, and conflict and repair.
introPoints: There are no perfect answers. The purpose is not to judge you, label you or decide whether you are ready for a relationship. It is to help you identify what is working well and where greater awareness or support may be useful.
Answer honestly, based on how you usually think, feel and behave in relationships—not how you wish you would behave.
This self-audit is a reflective tool, not a clinical diagnosis or a validated psychological test.

dimensions.title: Self-Knowledge
dimensions.description: Understanding your emotions, triggers and responses.
dimensions.guidance: Explore emotional triggers, recurring reactions and the experiences that may shape your expectations.
questions: I can recognise my emotional triggers before they strongly influence how I respond to my partner.
I can distinguish between what is happening in my relationship now and what past experiences may be bringing up for me.
When something upsets me, I can usually identify and communicate what I am feeling within a reasonable time.

dimensions.title: Emotional Regulation
dimensions.description: Managing difficult emotions without harming the relationship.
dimensions.guidance: Practise naming emotions, pausing when overwhelmed and returning to difficult conversations constructively.
questions: When I feel hurt or upset, I can express my feelings without attacking my partner or withdrawing completely.
I can listen to feedback from my partner without immediately becoming defensive or counterattacking.
I take responsibility for managing my emotions rather than expecting my partner to fix them for me.

dimensions.title: Inherited Patterns
dimensions.description: Recognising how earlier experiences shape present relationships.
dimensions.guidance: Identify which relationship lessons you want to retain, reconsider or leave behind.
questions: I understand how the relationships I witnessed growing up influence my expectations of a partner today.
I have consciously identified at least one unhealthy relationship pattern I do not want to repeat.
I have reflected on what previous relationships have taught me, including any patterns I may have contributed to.

dimensions.title: Capacity and Readiness
dimensions.description: Making room for a relationship while maintaining your own wellbeing.
dimensions.guidance: Reflect on your emotional availability, boundaries, responsibilities and expectations of a relationship.
questions: I can make room for a partner's needs while maintaining my own wellbeing, responsibilities and boundaries.
I can recognise when I am expecting a relationship to solve problems that require attention in other areas of my life.
I have people I trust who can offer honest feedback, and I am willing to consider their perspectives.

dimensions.title: Conflict and Repair
dimensions.description: Addressing disagreements, taking responsibility and rebuilding trust.
dimensions.guidance: Develop the ability to address difficult issues, acknowledge harm, rebuild trust and demonstrate change through behaviour.
questions: When I hurt someone, I can acknowledge the impact of my actions without immediately becoming defensive.
I can raise difficult issues before resentment builds or the situation becomes a crisis.
When I recognise that I have contributed to a problem, I make a genuine effort to change my behaviour, not just apologise.

safety.question: Has anything in your current or recent relationship made you feel unsafe—physically, sexually, emotionally or financially?

bands.label: An Area to Explore
bands.summary: Your responses suggest that this area may deserve more attention and reflection.

bands.label: Developing Awareness
bands.summary: You may recognise some helpful patterns while finding others difficult to sustain.

bands.label: A Growing Strength
bands.summary: You report several helpful habits, although circumstances can still challenge them.

bands.label: A Reported Strength
bands.summary: You identify these habits as consistent parts of how you approach relationships.

selfAudit.bandsNote: These are descriptive feedback bands for reflection, not validated clinical cut-offs or comparisons with other people.

nextStep.title: Start Where It Matters Most
nextStep.body: Start with the dimension that would make the greatest difference to your relationships if you strengthened it. You do not need to work on everything at once.

selfAudit.printNote: You can reflect on your results privately without booking a session. If you would like professional support to explore them further, I would be happy to help you identify a suitable next step.
disclaimer: This self-audit is an educational and reflective tool. It does not provide a clinical diagnosis, determine relationship compatibility or establish whether someone is ready for marriage. Its scoring system is not a validated psychometric measure.
A person's score should not be used to determine whether they should stay in or leave a relationship, particularly where abuse or safety concerns are present.
The results are intended to encourage self-awareness and support constructive conversations about relationships.

relationalRisk.name: The Relational Risk Assessment
relationalRisk.headline: A reflective check-in on the health of your relationship
relationalRisk.metaDescription: A free reflective check-in on five areas that influence the health and stability of a relationship. Private, browser-based, no sign-up required.
relationalRisk.siblingBlurb: A reflective check-in on the health of your relationship, across five areas that influence its health and stability.
intro: Every relationship has areas of strength and areas that need attention. Sometimes the difficulties are obvious. At other times, they develop gradually through unresolved disagreements, unclear boundaries, emotional distance, or patterns neither partner has fully examined.
The Relational Risk Assessment is designed to help you reflect on five areas that influence the health and stability of a relationship.
introPoints: This assessment is free and takes approximately 5–10 minutes.
Answer honestly, based on what usually happens in your relationship rather than what you hope happens.
There are no perfect answers. The purpose is awareness, not judgement.

This is a reflective tool, not a clinical diagnosis or a validated psychometric assessment. It is intended to support an honest conversation with yourself, your partner, or a relationship professional.
relationalRisk.scaleHelp: Choose the answer that best describes your relationship.

dimensions.title: Personal Patterns and Accountability
dimensions.description: Our individual histories, expectations, and habits influence how we relate to one another. Understanding our own contribution can help us respond more intentionally.
questions: Both of us have taken time to examine how our upbringing and past experiences influence our relationship.
When something goes wrong between us, each of us can recognise our own contribution rather than placing all the blame on the other person.
Neither of us expects our partner to heal personal wounds or solve problems that require individual responsibility.

dimensions.title: Conflict and Repair
dimensions.description: Disagreements are a normal part of relationships. What matters is whether partners can address them respectfully and find their way back to one another.
questions: After a serious disagreement, we have a reliable way of reconnecting and addressing what happened.
We return to unresolved disagreements within a reasonable time rather than allowing silence or resentment to continue for days or weeks.
Either of us can apologise, acknowledge hurt, or make a genuine effort to repair the relationship without feeling that doing so means losing power.

dimensions.title: Boundaries and Outside Influences
dimensions.description: Healthy relationships require clear boundaries with family members, friends, former partners, and other people whose opinions or involvement may affect the relationship.
questions: We have clear and mutually understood boundaries regarding the involvement of extended family and other people in our relationship.
We discuss significant relationship concerns with each other before involving someone outside the relationship, except when seeking appropriate support or help for safety reasons.
Past relationships, unresolved attachments, or outside opinions do not routinely interfere with the trust and decisions we are building together.

dimensions.title: Communication and Emotional Connection
dimensions.description: Emotional distance can develop even when partners live together, fulfil their responsibilities, and appear to be getting along. Honest communication helps prevent unspoken concerns from becoming lasting disconnection.
questions: I can raise concerns that bother me instead of routinely keeping quiet to avoid an uncomfortable conversation.
We can discuss important or sensitive subjects without one or both of us consistently shutting down, withdrawing, or refusing to engage.
Our quiet periods generally reflect genuine peace and comfort rather than unresolved tension, emotional distance, or fear of raising difficult issues.

dimensions.title: Intentional Relationship Review
dimensions.description: Healthy relationships benefit from deliberate attention. Regular conversations help partners notice changes and address concerns before they become harder to resolve.
questions: We deliberately discuss the state of our relationship, rather than talking only about responsibilities, finances, household matters, or children.
Within the past six months, we have had meaningful conversations about important areas such as money, intimacy, expectations, and our future together.
When something begins to change between us, we make an effort to recognise it early and discuss it before the distance grows.

safety.eyebrow: One important question about your safety
safety.question: Has anything in your current relationship made you feel unsafe — physically, sexually, emotionally, or financially?

bands.label: An area needing attention
bands.summary: The habits or practices covered by this dimension may be inconsistent or underdeveloped. Consider what is making this area difficult and what needs to change.

bands.label: An area developing in strength
bands.summary: Some helpful habits are present, but they may not be reliable under stress. Greater consistency and intentional effort may help.

bands.label: A growing strength
bands.summary: This area appears to have a reasonably strong foundation, although there may still be situations that require attention.

bands.label: A reported strength
bands.summary: Your responses suggest that the habits covered by this dimension are well established. Continue to nurture them, particularly during periods of stress or change.

relationalRisk.bandsNote: These bands are reflective guides, not clinical cut-offs or validated measures of relationship risk.
resultsIntro: Your responses offer a snapshot of how you experience your relationship today. They are not a prediction of whether your relationship will succeed or fail.

Look beyond the overall score. The individual dimensions may reveal more about where your relationship feels secure, where helpful habits are developing, and where a more intentional conversation could make a difference.
A lower score is an invitation to explore, not a verdict on your relationship.

nextStep.title: Your next step
nextStep.body: Understanding your relationship is a starting point. What matters next is deciding what deserves attention and how to address it constructively. If your results raise questions or highlight recurring difficulties, you may choose to book a relationship conversation with Dr Lauretta Ogbum to explore your concerns and identify an appropriate way forward.

disclaimer: This assessment is a reflective instrument, not a clinical diagnosis, and has not been psychometrically validated. It is designed to support awareness and conversation, not to determine the future of a relationship.
